documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into embodied robotic planning, yet standard benchmarks primarily evaluate end-to-end task completion in nominal environments, obscuring failure origins across the execution stack. We present Alpha, a systematic fault-injection and robustness-evaluation framework for LLM-driven manipulation in simulation. Alpha injects calibrated faults across perception (sensor lag), actuation (grip slip), kinematics (unreachable targets), and planning (planner-output corruption), alongside concurrent conditions. To separate physical vulnerabilities from planner sensitivities, we introduce a matched methodology pairing an LLM agent (Llama-3 via Ollama) against a deterministic Scripted Oracle planner across a balanced 150-episode matrix under identical seeds, geometries, and safety criteria. Across the matrix, the Oracle achieves 64.0% (48/75) success while the LLM achieves 44.0% (33/75) (paired McNemar p = 3.01 x 10^-4). Crucially, excluding planner-output corruption, performance across all physical and kinematic conditions is identical: 55.0% (33/60) for both planners with zero discordant pairs (McNemar p = 1.00). This demonstrates that physical actuator slip, kinematic reach boundaries, and perceptual staleness affect deterministic controllers and LLM planners equivalently. The performance gap is driven entirely by planner-output corruption (100% Oracle vs. 0% LLM), isolating the prompt-to-JSON serialization and validation interface rather than a cognitive reasoning deficit. We also audit 169 historical pilot attempts for transparency.

The growing sophistication and need to have sustainable energy systems has led to the shift of the conventional power grids to smart power grids. Such grids are equipped with innovative technologies that include digital communication, Internet of Things (IoT), and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to increase the efficiency, reliability, and scalability of energy delivery. This paper introduce an AI-based approach to smart power grid management, with the emphasis on the incorporation of an autonomous and controllable intelligent service hub that would be able to process multimodal data, such as textual reports, images, videos, and sensor data. The framework applies AI methods of machine learning, deep learning, and predictive analytics to optimize energy allocation, faults, and failure prediction with minimum human intervention. With real-time analysis, the system dynamically changes the operation of the grids with incoming data, enhancing energy efficiency and lowering the cost of operations by up to 30 percent, between $12,000 and 8,400 in the example of energy optimization. Also, the fault detection system shows a remarkable accuracy of 0.97 in terms of AUC whereas the predictive maintenance model reports an accuracy rate of 95.5. The balancing nature of the energy demand and generation provided by the framework is critical in integrating renewable energy sources since it can help in countering the problem of intermittency of the solar and wind energy. Moreover, the system has a multimodal document processing feature that increases decision-making through the synthesis of various types of data and provides a more detailed overview of grid work. This paper explains how the suggested AI-based framework can greatly improve the efficiency, reliability, and sustainability of smart power grids, which will result in the future improvements in energy management.

Radiation treatment planning requires balancing competing objectives to satisfy clinical criteria while accommodating physicians' preferences. This study aims to develop an evidence-driven, multi-agent compound AI system that integrates DRL-based automated treatment planning with LLM-based conversational plan refinement for proton PBS therapy. A policy network trained using PPO first generates multiple plans without human intervention, from which one is selected as the target plan and the others serve as references for subsequent refinements. For challenging cases requiring further adjustments, an LLM-based multi-agent system enables plan refinement through natural language interactions. The system comprises a planning agent that recommends evidence-supported adjustments, a chatbot providing a unified conversational interface, and an evaluation agent that retrieves clinical metrics and identifies constraint violations. To enhance domain-specific reasoning, the planning agent based on Qwen3-14B is designed to justify its recommendations using evidence from previously generated plans and post-trained on task-specific data using SFT and GRPO. The framework was trained and evaluated using 21 patients with H&N cancers, with 5 PPO-generated plans per patient. Of these, 50 plans were selected for instruction-guided refinement. Compared with the base LLM, the post-trained Qwen3-14B demonstrated improved instruction-following, information retrieval and domain-specific reasoning capabilities. The resulting adjustments more effectively improved user-prioritized objectives while limiting deterioration in competing objectives, yielding more clinically appropriate trade-offs in patient-specific plan refinement. The proposed compound AI system provides a user-friendly planning platform, offering a promising approach to personalized proton PBS treatment planning.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) comprises diverse neurodevelopmental conditions with symptoms differing based on genetics, development, age, and other factors.Detecting ASD has challenges as symptoms often manifest in early life and can lead to delayed analysis.Because standard diagnostic practices rely heavily on human interpretation, making it prone to bias and inefficiency.To attain objective and effective detection, machine learning (ML) methods have become increasingly valuable.Thus, there is a need for an enhanced and accurate ML method that can successfully handle feature selection (FS) and parameter tuning for ASD severity classification.Therefore, this study presents an Advanced Evolutionary Framework for Automated Autism Detection and Severity Classification (AEF-AADSC).The major aim of this work is to design an intelligent machine learning framework to classify autism spectrum disorder severity grading.Initially, the proposed undergoes preprocessing of the raw dataset to ensure high-quality input for the learning model through missing value handling, encoding, and normalization process.Subsequently, feature selection is carried out using an Improved Genetic Algorithm, which selects the most relevant features and thereby enhances model efficiency.The selected features are then utilized for training a CatBoost classifier for accurate classification of ASD severity levels.In addition, hyperparameter optimization is carried out using Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy to further enhance predictive performance.To improve model transparency and interpretability, Explainable artificial intelligence is incorporated using SHapley Additive exPlanations, enabling analysis of feature contributions and supporting better understanding of the classification decisions.The performance validation of the proposed approach is carried out using the Autism Diagnosis Based on Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)-5 dataset.The AEF-AADSC method achieves improved performance with an accuracy of 96.30% compared to baseline methods in terms of different measures.Therefore, the proposed model is found to be a robust approach for the automated ASD severity grading process.

The article addresses the problem of social management of medical personnel amid the digital transformation of healthcare and significant changes in the relationships among medical workers, patients, administrative structures, and digital systems. In response to current interdisciplinary shifts, an integrated model for managing medical personnel is proposed — one that accounts for macrosocial factors, mechanisms of social perception related to the profession, and aggregated indicators at the level of the workers’ subjective world. The methodological foundation is a systems approach, within which medical personnel are viewed as a social system shaped not only by linear macro-management influences but also by relevant public relations, images of the medical profession, the communication environment, the features of digital healthcare products etc. A three-level management model is substantiated, comprising the macro level of normative and organizational structures, the meso level of social perception, and the micro level of professional attitudes, loyalty, and motivation of personnel. It is shown that social perception serves a connecting function between macro-management decisions and actual professional practices. The article emphasizes the need to manage the images of medical personnel — including their reproduction in artificial intelligence — as well as to consider the psychological climate as a significant factor of loyalty. The proposed model makes it possible to increase the coherence of management goals, mechanisms, and interventions.

Early diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma is critical to preserve access to curative treatment options. The Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) provides a standardized framework for non-invasive diagnosis on multiphase computed tomography, based on major visual imaging features. However, these features may be difficult to assess consistently, particularly in small liver lesions. We developed dLI-RADS, an interpretable artificial intelligence method designed to estimate the probability of hepatocellular carcinoma from multiphase computed tomography images of manually segmented liver lesions, while remaining aligned with LI-RADS-related imaging concepts. dLI-RADS combines neural network-derived predictions with handcrafted quantitative imaging measurements reflecting LI-RADS major features and integrates these inputs using logistic regression. In this multicenter retrospective study, patients with multiphase computed tomography and at least one liver lesion were included, while lesions larger than 40 mm were excluded. Histology served as the reference standard for hepatocellular carcinoma, and a composite reference standard was used for non-hepatocellular carcinoma lesions. The lesion-level accuracy of dLI-RADS and LI-RADS were compared on the internal evaluation set using 10,000-repetition bootstrap non-inferiority tests, with 5% margins and significance levels. On the external test set, sensitivities were similarly compared. dLI-RADS was non-inferior to LI-RADS for lesion-level accuracy in the internal evaluation set, achieving 80% accuracy compared with 74% for LI-RADS (p = 0.04)...
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: The commercial application of generative artificial intelligence has rapidly brought to the fore the structural tension between machine-generated content (AIGC) and the core presuppositions of copyright law concerning the “author.” This paper examines the protection model and legal mechanisms adopted by the United States on the question of AIGC copyrightability. The research finds that the United States, as represented by the Thaler case, strengthens the “human authorship” requirement from the perspectives of constitutional text, statutory interpretation, and incentive theory, and adopts a result-oriented standard centered on expressive control.

Abstract Oxidative stress is a critical driver of various severe diseases, positioning antioxidant peptides (APs) as promising therapeutic agents. However, their discovery is constrained by the limitations of low-throughput wet-lab assays and insufficient computational prediction tools. To address this, we developed Antioxidant Peptides eXplorer (AOXP), a deep learning framework that leverages multiscale feature integration for high-precision AP prediction. Unlike existing models that often rely on isolated sequence patterns or manual feature descriptors, AOXP employs a hybrid encoding strategy that synergistically fuses deep, context-aware semantic representations from the protein large language model (ESM2) with explicit physicochemical and sequence distribution features. We constructed an optimized MLP architecture based on a refined 2400-dimensional feature vector, which was systematically benchmarked among five architectures and four feature selection strategies. Comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that AOXP achieves competitive performance across evaluation data sets, achieving a benchmark AUC of 0.736 on test_set1_drop and a sensitivity of 0.878 on the positive-only independent Test set 2, significantly outperforming current mainstream computational predictors in both sensitivity and robustness. Integrated Gradients analysis further quantified feature contributions, revealing that ESM2-derived semantics are the most influential features for model prediction (by feature number), followed by hydrophobicity, polarity, charge, and solvent accessibility. To demonstrate its therapeutic utility, AOXP was applied to screen a large peptide library targeting the Keap1-Nrf2 oxidative response pathway. A computationally predicted candidate peptide, MGRRHRHVTDEDDEENLGGDDDDGDDDVYMYPADMHPDERHAYREAV, was identified and validated through molecular dynamics simulations, exhibiting superior binding affinity for the Keap1 Kelch domain compared to the native ligand. AOXP provides a robust and efficient framework for the discovery of functional antioxidant peptides (available at: http://aidd.bioai-global.com/AOXP/).

Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) are increasingly being applied to support data-driven decision-making in food processing, quality control, and food safety. This review provides a critical assessment of recent technological advances and examines how AI models are being integrated with computer vision, spectroscopy, hyperspectral imaging (HSI), biosensors, Internet of Things (IoT) platforms, and intelligent monitoring systems throughout the food value chain. This review brings together evidence from academic studies and industry-based research to examine how AI is currently used in the food sector. The applications considered include process control and optimization, fermentation management, quality grading, authenticity assessment, shelf-life prediction, contaminant detection, and support for food-safety decisions. Recent research extends beyond conventional prediction toward adaptive decision support and, in a smaller number of cases, partially autonomous food systems. Approaches such as explainable AI, multimodal learning, foundation models, digital twins, intelligent packaging, and agentic AI are being investigated for real-time monitoring, data integration, and production management. Their level of maturity, however, varies considerably, and many applications remain conceptual or confined to laboratory settings. Data heterogeneity, poor transferability, limited external validation, and regulatory uncertainty continue to restrict industrial adoption. Although one industrial-scale drying study reported a 12.8% reduction in energy consumption, external validation of food-quality models has resulted in markedly higher prediction errors. This contrast illustrates the difficulty of transferring performance from controlled datasets to new products or production environments. Rather than examining these technologies separately, this review considers their roles across food processing, quality control, and food safety, together with the evidence for industrial validation, sustainability, and governance. Further progress will depend on whether models remain reliable outside their development datasets, not simply on incremental gains in internally reported accuracy.

Background Artificial intelligence is transforming agro-export management by converting production, commercial, climate, and logistics data into support for more timely decisions. In Latin America, however, evidence on its managerial applications and contribution to sustainable operations remains fragmented. Objective To synthesize evidence on the application of artificial intelligence to managerial decision-making and its contribution to the efficiency, sustainability, traceability, resilience, and competitiveness of sustainable agro-export operations in Latin America from 1996 to 2025. Methods A systematic review and bibliometric analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020. Scopus and Web of Science yielded 2160 records; after filtering, screening, and eligibility assessment, 73 studies were included. Bibliometrix in RStudio and VOSviewer were used to analyze scientific production, authors, countries, sources, Bradford’s and Lotka’s laws, keyword co-occurrence, and thematic clusters. Results Scientific output increased markedly after 2021 and peaked in 2024. Scopus accounted for 98.95% of the records. China led with 170 publications, while Brazil, with 149, was the only Latin American country among the five most productive. Four thematic areas were identified: prediction and classification using artificial intelligence and machine learning; logistics, supply chains, and suppliers; sustainable resource management and climate risks; and digital transformation through Agriculture 4.0/5.0. Across the literature, artificial intelligence was found to reduce uncertainty and improve decision-making, although its effectiveness depends on data quality, digital infrastructure, and organizational capabilities. Conclusions Artificial intelligence represents a strategic capability for strengthening sustainable agro-export operations. Its impact depends on integrating algorithms with reliable data, technological infrastructure, organizational capabilities, and sustainability criteria. The limited representation of Latin America highlights the need for further empirical research adapted to regional conditions.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Wearable electronics represent a transformative shift in the integration of digital technology with the human body, enabling continuous monitoring, enhanced interactivity, and real-time data acquisition in a compact, user-friendly form. These devices, ranging from smartwatches and fitness trackers to smart textiles and implantable biosensors, have revolutionized healthcare, fitness, communication, and entertainment. By offering real-time physiological monitoring, wearables have opened new frontiers in personalized medicine, chronic disease management, and remote diagnostics. Beyond health, wearable technologies are redefining human–machine interaction in sectors such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), defense, industrial safety, and sports performance optimization. Looking forward, the convergence of flexible electronics, nanomaterials, energy harvesting, and artificial intelligence is propelling wearables beyond traditional formats. Next-generation devices aim for seamless skin integration, biodegradability, self-healing materials, and neural interfacing—pushing the boundaries of cyber-physical symbiosis. These advancements point toward a future where wearables transition from external gadgets to embedded, intelligent systems capable of enhancing cognition, perception, and human capability in real time. This abstract outlines the current applications and explores the trajectory of wearable electronics as they evolve from assistive devices to integral components of the human body, fundamentally reshaping our interaction with technology and the environment.
topics: Advanced Sensor and Energy Harvesting Materials

documents.abstract: Why large language models trained via log-loss minimization over massive and diverse datasets exhibit broad capabilities and generalizable skills is not yet fully understood. Grau-Moya et al. (ICML 2024) offer a conceptual explanation through the lens of meta-learning: if sequence-generating environments $ν$ are drawn from a prior $w_ν$, minimizing population log-loss recovers the corresponding Bayesian mixture predictor $ξ=\sum_νw_νν$. In the idealized limit in which $w$ is a universal prior, the optimal predictor corresponds to Solomonoff universal induction. Practical machine learning algorithms, however, generally produce only \emph{approximately} optimal predictors. This raises a natural question: \emph{Does the prediction performance remain robust under approximation}? In this paper, we first provide a tight bound on the worst-case effect of approximation on prediction error. We show any predictor $ρ$ satisfying $D_{KL}(ξ\|ρ)\leq η$ retains bounded cumulative-expected-squared prediction error. However, while the Bayesian mixture predictor $ξ$ has error $O(\log(1/w_μ))$ in an environment $μ$, we establish a tight $Θ(η/w_μ)$ bound on the excess error of $ρ$ relative to $ξ$. Thus, approximation can substantially degrade performance in environments assigned small prior probability. In sharp contrast, when environments are averaged according to prior $w$, we prove that the excess prediction error is only $O(η)$. Furthermore, we establish a distribution-shift theorem for dominated shifts from a training prior $w$ to a test prior $w'$, interpolating our average-case and worst-case guarantees. Finally, we extend our robustness analysis to a finite-sampling setting relevant to learning universal predictors with neural networks and Transformers, where $D_{KL}(ξ\|ρ)$ could be unbounded. [For the full abstract, see the paper.]

Training Arabic large language models faces challenges from noisy web data, dialectal variation, and the high cost of continual pretraining (CPT). We introduce AQL-Lite (AQL: Arabic Quality Language), a time- and resource-efficient framework for adapting a multilingual LLM to Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). AQL-Lite couples a quality-first curation pipeline (structural cleaning, heuristic and model-based filtering, MSA selection, and deduplication) with a partial-parameter CPT recipe that trains RS-LoRA adapters across the network together with the last eight transformer blocks and the embedding matrix, under layer-wise learning rates. At a matched 1B-token budget, CPT on AQL-curated data raises a four-benchmark Arabic mean by 3.51 points over CPT on raw web text, which yields no gain over the base model. In a controlled 5B-token comparison, AQL-Lite recovers 94% of the gain of full-parameter CPT (mean 73.19 vs. 73.58) in 52% of the wall-clock time and outperforms adapter-only baselines on every benchmark, and a component ablation shows that adapters, unfrozen blocks, and embedding training each contribute. Scaled to 40B MSA tokens and instruction-tuned on one million examples, the resulting 12B model scores 75.3 on the seven-benchmark Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard v2 (OALL v2) suite. These results suggest that partial-parameter CPT on a carefully curated corpus is a practical route to efficient MSA adaptation.

Water quality assessment is essential for determining whether water is suitable for human consumption and enabling informed decision-making regarding water resources. Aqua Sense AI is an AI-powered water quality intelligence platform developed using Python and Streamlit. The system provides a preliminary classification of water samples as Safe (Potable) or Unsafe (Non-Potable) based on nine physicochemical parameters: pH, Hardness, Total Dissolved Solids (TDS), Chloramines, Sulfate, Conductivity, Organic Carbon, Trihalomethanes, and Turbidity. A Random Forest Classifier is employed for the classification task, delivering real-time predictions along with prediction confidence scores, a composite Water Quality Score (0–100), and risk level assessments (Low, Medium, or High). Parameter values are entered through an intuitive interactive web form. The platform features an Analytics Dashboard powered by interactive Plotly visualizations, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) providing feature importance rankings and natural language reasoning, dynamic parameter-specific water treatment recommendations, and session-based prediction history tracking. Designed in alignment with UN Sustainable Development Goal 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), the system serves as a preliminary decision-support tool and does not replace certified laboratory testing. Overall, the work demonstrates an integrated approach that combines machine learning, explainability, interactive data analytics, and actionable guidance within a unified water quality assessment platform
topics: Data Mining and Machine Learning Applications

documents.abstract: Analogical reasoning is widely considered a fundamental component of human intelligence. Few benchmarks are designed to explicitly test far analogical reasoning - reasoning between domains that are superficially dissimilar yet share deep relational or structural similarities. In this work, we introduce an analogical reasoning benchmark called Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus of ANAlogy (ARCANA). The tasks of ARCANA require performing far analogical mappings from real-world objects or physical phenomena to abstract grid-based transformations, different from the well-known ARC-AGI benchmark which primarily emphasized innate human priors. We validate ARCANA through a human study, demonstrating that humans solve these tasks reliably. In contrast, evaluations across a range of large language models show a distinct performance gap compared to humans, revealing systematic failure modes that remain challenging for current models. To address this gap, we propose ConceptSIR, a reasoning framework based on concept slippage, introspection, and reflection. Experiments demonstrate that ConceptSIR enables standard LLMs to solve several challenging ARCANA tasks that were unsolved by direct prompting in our evaluation. Overall, our results suggest that far analogical reasoning remains an open problem for contemporary LLMs. All the materials are available at sites.google.com/view/arcanacogtest. The complete codebase, including benchmark, and ConceptSIR, is publicly available at https://github.com/density-11/arcana-test. All ARCANA data and task instances can be accessed and explored at https://arcanacogtest.org/.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing architectural design through generative modelling, performance prediction, spatial planning, and workflow automation. However, many current applications address individual tasks or emphasize visual novelty, while practical design decisions must balance human needs, climate responsiveness, affordability, accessibility, regulatory constraints, and environmental performance. This paper proposes a Human-Centered and Sustainability-Aware AI Architectural Design Framework (HCS-AADF) that combines these considerations within an iterative design-support workflow. The framework accepts user requirements, site and climate information, budget limits, and applicable design constraints; analyses the project context; generates alternative layouts or massing concepts; evaluates alternatives against multiple criteria; explains trade-offs; and returns shortlisted options to an architect for review. Human feedback can be used to refine subsequent iterations. A conceptual multi-criteria scoring model and an evaluation protocol are specified to support future implementation and testing. The paper synthesizes three supplied research directions—AI architectures informed by human drives and emotions, the adoption and capabilities of AI software tools in architecture, and systematic reviews of AI applications in architectural design—along with relevant recent literature on generative design and sustainable building optimization. The proposed contribution is an integrated, transparent workflow rather than a claim of experimentally proven performance. Expected benefits include more traceable design comparisons, earlier consideration of sustainability, and improved collaboration between architects and AI systems. The framework also identifies risks involving data quality, bias, explainability, regulatory verification, and over-reliance on generated outputs. Experimental validation with representative building projects and expert review is proposed as the next step.

Incorporation of artificial intelligence in the process of creative writing entails a paradigmatic change in literary text production, assessment, and perception. In this research paper, the focus is made on an innovative role of large language models in the sphere of English language and literature authorship. Based on systematic analysis of recent empirical studies and theoretical approaches, three interrelated aspects will be discussed: interaction between human authors and AI systems, reception of artificial literature by the readership, and conceptualization of authorship in the digital age. For the purpose of this paper, the mixed-method approach involving both quantitative analysis of empirical studies and qualitative analysis of literary theoretical approaches will be used. As the results of the analysis indicate, the texts generated by AI are rated aesthetically the same way as texts written by human authors when there is no indication of the author's identity; however, readers maintain biases against texts that are perceived to be machine-generated.

Artificial Intelligence, virtual reality, and augmented reality are reshaping how interior design students think, explore, and communicate ideas. This chapter examines how emerging technologies expand creative capacity, accelerate iteration, and strengthen evidence-based decision-making across all phases of the design process, from programming and concept development to design development, construction documents, and client communication. Through examples, workflows, and case studies, the chapter shows how AI can enhance analysis, visualization, and performance testing while preserving human authorship, ethics, and critical judgment. Students learn how to integrate AI strategically, document its use responsibly, and maintain conceptual clarity and design intent in a rapidly evolving digital studio environment.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in electric power and energy systems for forecasting, fault diagnosis, stability assessment, control, renewable energy integration, and real-time monitoring. However, evidence remains fragmented across algorithms, applications, performance metrics, and deployment conditions. This study reviews recent AI applications in power and energy systems and examines their technological, economic, and operational contributions and limitations. A PRISMA-based systematic and bibliometric review was conducted using Scopus and Web of Science records published from 2021 to 2025. Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny 5.5.0 and VOSviewer 1.6.20 were used to analyze publication trends, citation patterns, geographical distribution, influential studies, and keyword networks, while 40 studies were retained for systematic evidence synthesis. In the reconciled 4854-record corpus, annual scientific production increased from 610 publications in 2021 to 1305 in 2025, with research concentrating on machine learning, deep learning, smart grids, stability, renewable energy, forecasting, fault diagnosis, optimization, and cybersecurity. The reviewed studies reported improvements in predictive accuracy, computational efficiency, fault localization, voltage control, energy savings, and real-time decision support. Nevertheless, data dependence, computational cost, limited interpretability, simulation-to-field transfer, and validation requirements remain major barriers. Future research should prioritize robust, explainable, physics-aware, and field-validated AI for critical power-system applications.

Blood culture contamination classifiers are typically benchmarked against microbiological reference labels that encode collection-site skin antisepsis timing as an unmeasured confounder, so reported specificity and safety metrics may reflect the labelling process rather than classifier behaviour. the present analysis formalises the problem as a before-after-control-impact design in which the estimand is the interaction between classifier deployment and an antisepsis-timing regime, and characterises the operating characteristics of that design under a declared variance structure. Using a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5 and an intraclass correlation of 0.640, power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design required 54 clusters to detect a 5-percentage-point interaction at 80% power, a requirement that exceeds the cluster counts examined and that exposes the fragility of single-site classifier benchmarks. The paper derives the bias in apparent specificity when antisepsis timing is omitted, states the conditions under which the before-after-control-impact interaction identifies the classifier-attributable effect, and argues that contamination-classifier safety claims should be reported as design-bounded rather than as intrinsic properties of the model.
topics: Clinical Laboratory Practices and Quality Control

documents.abstract: Verbal autopsy (VA) remains the principal source of cause-of-death labels for community health worker (CHW) triage algorithms in low-resource settings, yet the recall interval between death and VA interview is rarely recorded and almost never modelled. the present analysis treats unmeasured recall decay as a structured label-noise process and characterises the operating characteristics of a before-after-control-impact (BACII) benchmarking design used to evaluate CHW triage classifiers under that noise. No observational data are used or claimed: the analysis is a replication-based evaluation of the estimator under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.640), with power estimated across 2000 design cells spanning cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design attains 80% power at 54 clusters for a 5-percentage-point effect. The paper derives a bias bound showing that recall decay inflates the apparent between-cluster variance component and therefore the intraclass correlation, and it proposes a sensitivity-analysis protocol that reports benchmarking conclusions as a function of an assumed decay rate rather than as a single point estimate. The contribution is a design-level account of how label noise that is unmeasured but structurally bounded can be made visible in AI benchmarking for healthcare, together with the sample-size consequences of that visibility.

Drug-drug interaction alert suppression in district formularies depends on renal function estimates that are themselves rounded before they reach the rule engine, and the safety consequences of that rounding are rarely quantified. the present analysis treats alert suppression as a decision rule operating on a discretised renal covariate and derives the operating characteristics of a before-after-control-impact design for evaluating suppression policies under unmeasured assay rounding. The design is characterised analytically and by a replication-based power analysis across 2000 design cells, with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64. Power curves, minimum detectable effect curves, a kernel density of estimated power, coefficient intervals, a power-versus-cluster scatter and a residual diagnostic are reported for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Fifty-two clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point change at 80 per cent power. The contribution is a formal statement of the rounding-induced bias in suppression thresholds and a design-level account of how that bias propagates into benchmark estimates, with implications for how district formularies should report renal covariates to artificial intelligence safety benchmarks.

Emergency department triage classifiers are benchmarked almost exclusively on static acuity labels, yet the operational label is produced when a nurse re-scores a patient at queue reordering. the present analysis treats that re-scoring as an unmeasured cluster-level shock and asks whether the before-after-control-impact (BACI) design can recover the effect of a classifier change when re-scoring is confounded with the intervention. A replication-based evaluation was conducted over a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, using 2000 replications per design cell across 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Power reached 80% at 52 clusters for a 5-percentage-point effect; at the largest design cell of 32 clusters the minimum detectable effect remained above the 5-point target. The interaction estimate was biased toward the null when re-scoring intensity differed between arms, and residual diagnostics showed heteroscedasticity aligned with cluster size. The contribution is a stability bound: BACI benchmarking of triage classifiers is defensible only when re-scoring is either measured or shown to be exchangeable across arms, and the paper specifies the design conditions under which that claim can be tested.

Cholera forecast models that combine rainfall drivers with ensemble machine learning are increasingly proposed as decision aids for outbreak preparedness, yet their evaluation typically assumes that sanitation covariates are observed without delay. The framework formalises reporting lag as a latent state that decouples the covariate process from the decision time, defines a lag-robust ensemble aggregator, and derives a decision-value bound that separates forecast discrimination from the economic cost of acting on stale sanitation information. Using NASA POWER monthly reanalysis air temperature at 2 m for Kampala (0.35, 32.58) over 2000-2023, comprising 312 monthly observations with a mean of 22.443 C and a linear trend of -0.1564 C per decade, the paper demonstrates how the benchmarking protocol is operationalised on a real covariate stream. The contribution is a reproducible evaluation design that reports decision value rather than accuracy alone, and that makes the reporting-lag assumption an explicit object of benchmarking rather than a hidden modelling convenience.

Federated learning promises to train sepsis early-warning models across district hospitals without centralising patient data, but the label noise generated by heterogeneous local coding practices threatens both the validity and the fairness of the resulting models. The framework specifies a before-after-control-impact design with a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.640) and characterises the operating characteristics of the design across 2000 replications per cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power, and it derives the bias and coverage consequences of site-heterogeneous label noise for federated averaging. The contribution is a reproducible audit protocol that separates the statistical power of the evaluation design from the fairness properties of the model being evaluated, so that benchmarking claims about federated sepsis models can be stated with explicit boundary conditions.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) are increasingly proposed for triage across inter-facility referral networks, yet their safety evaluation typically assumes that transport times between facilities are observed. In many low- and middle-income referral systems, transport time is unmeasured and right-censored: only the fact that a patient arrived, or did not, is recorded. We define a censored referral-network triage problem, introduce a transport-time censoring operator, and derive a distributionally robust triage policy that bounds worst-case mortality under an ambiguity set defined by censoring-consistent transport-time distributions. We prove that the robust policy admits a tractable convex reformulation and that its safety gap relative to the oracle policy is bounded by the Wasserstein radius of the ambiguity set. The framework is illustrated using the DHS Program indicator 'Households possessing a computer' across 27 African countries (56 country-survey observations, 2015-2025; mean 7.893, SD 5.144), which serves as a proxy for digital readiness of referral nodes. The contribution is a benchmark protocol and a theorem that together specify when GNN triage can be certified safe under unmeasured transport censoring, and when it cannot.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Sepsis early-warning models trained on nurse-collected vital signs inherit a temporal defect that benchmarking practice has not yet named: the interval between a bedside observation and its transcription into the electronic record varies with shift handover and is never measured. the present analysis treats that unmeasured lag as a design parameter rather than a nuisance and asks what benchmarking conclusions about artificial-intelligence sepsis onset prediction remain defensible when the lag is acknowledged. The analysis is a replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), with power estimated across 2000 design cells at cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design required 54 clusters to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The results show that the intraclass correlation of 0.64 dominates the operating characteristics: at 8 clusters no effect size in the design grid reached 80% power, and the minimum detectable effect at 80% power fell steeply as clusters increased from 8 to 32. Benchmarking claims for sepsis early-warning models are conditional on a design that can absorb the lag, and it specifies the cluster counts and effect sizes at which such claims become defensible.

Sparse-sensing continuous glucose monitors supply the input stream for most deployed insulin-dosing forecasters, yet the meal-announcement channel those forecasters rely on is systematically incomplete in free-living use. the present analysis treats unmeasured meal-announcement noncompliance as a design property of the evaluation, not a nuisance to be imputed away, and asks what a safety-regret benchmark can identify when the announcement indicator is missing not at random. A formal framework is developed in which the forecaster's action set, the announcement-compliance process and the hypoglycaemia loss are defined jointly, and a regret functional is derived that bounds the safety cost of benchmarking on the observed announcement channel alone. The framework is characterised analytically under a before-after-control-impact design with an intraclass correlation of 0.64, a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and a residual standard deviation of 4.5; under that variance structure, 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power, and power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis yields three results: an identification bound showing that observed-channel benchmarking understates regret by a factor that grows with the noncompliance rate; a design theorem giving the cluster count at which the bound is dominated by sampling error rather than by noncompliance bias; and a reporting protocol that makes the noncompliance assumption auditable. The contribution is a benchmark design that treats announcement noncompliance as a first-class safety parameter rather than a preprocessing step.

Sparse-view dental cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) reconstruction with deep learning promises dose reduction, but clinical deployment is threatened by unmeasured patient motion that corrupts projection geometry in ways no benchmark currently captures. The design was evaluated across 2000 replications per cell over cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD of 6.0, residual SD of 4.5 and intraclass correlation of 0.64. Power analysis indicated that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The framework distinguishes motion-agnostic, motion-aware and motion-robust benchmarking regimes, and shows that the BACI estimator's operating characteristics degrade sharply below 24 clusters. The contribution is a design-level account of what a defensible motion-robustness benchmark must measure, and a quantified statement of the sample sizes at which such benchmarks can distinguish reconstruction quality from noise.

Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is increasingly used to predict Mycobacterium tuberculosis drug resistance, and machine-learning classifiers trained on WGS data are benchmarked against phenotypic drug-susceptibility testing (DST). A persistent obstacle to fair benchmarking is mixed-strain heteroresistance: within a single patient, subpopulations of bacilli may carry different resistance mutations, so the phenotype recorded by DST is a population-level summary that does not correspond to any single genome. We define the calibration gap as the difference between the classifier's predicted probability of resistance and the probability that a randomly selected bacillus in the population is resistant, and we show that under a two-strain mixture model the gap is bounded by a function of the minor-variant allele frequency and the classifier's discriminative capacity. The framework is evaluated in a design study using a before-after-control-impact variance structure with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64; power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 56 clusters are required for 80% power at a 5-percentage-point effect. We argue that calibration, not discrimination alone, should be the primary benchmark for WGS-based resistance prediction, and we specify the reporting standards that would make heteroresistance-aware benchmarking reproducible.

Verbal autopsy (VA) remains the primary source of cause-of-death information for under-five mortality in settings without complete civil registration, yet the cause labels it produces are known to be misclassified in ways that are rarely quantified and almost never propagated into the machine-learning pipelines that consume them. We define a misclassification operator on the label simplex, derive the bias it induces in ensemble risk scores and in decision-curve net benefit, and show that the ranking of ensembles by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve is invariant to symmetric label noise only under restrictive conditions that fail for the asymmetric confusion structures typical of VA. The framework is illustrated with a decision-curve evaluation protocol that separates ensemble discrimination, calibration and clinical utility, and that reports the range of misclassification rates over which a given ensemble ranking is preserved. We argue that benchmarking practice in this domain should report a misclassification-robustness envelope alongside conventional performance metrics, and we specify the sensitivity analysis that such reporting requires. The contribution is methodological: it does not report new empirical results but provides the formal apparatus and reporting standard needed before ensemble comparisons on VA-derived labels can be interpreted as evidence about clinical decision quality.

Community health worker (CHW) programmes are widely used to support hypertension control, but the visit logs that record CHW contacts are frequently incomplete, and this incompleteness is not random: patients who are lost to follow-up, disengaged, or transferred between facilities are systematically less likely to have their visits recorded. The framework combines an augmented inverse-probability-weighted (AIPW) estimator with a completeness model that reweights the observed visit records to the target population, and it is evaluated through a replication-based design study of the before-after-control-impact (BACI) estimator under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64). Power was estimated across 2000 design cells for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design required 54 clusters to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The contribution is a formal identification result for the CHW visit effect under log incompleteness, together with a design-analysis characterisation of the BACI estimator that quantifies how cluster count and effect size jointly determine detectable effects in outreach-targeting evaluations.

White-coat measurement confounding threatens the validity of artificial-intelligence-guided hypertension treatment escalation in community clinics: when the decision to intensify therapy is informed by a blood pressure reading that is itself distorted by the measurement setting, the prescribing rule and the outcome share a common cause that no observed covariate set captures. No observational data are used or claimed. The analysis declares a variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, and estimates power across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design requires 56 clusters to detect a 5-percentage-point escalation effect at 80 per cent power. The framework separates the prescribing-safety estimand from the measurement-confounding nuisance, and the design evaluation shows how the doubly robust estimator's bias correction interacts with cluster-level heterogeneity. The contribution is a formal statement of the identification conditions under which an AI prescribing rule can be evaluated for safety when white-coat measurement is unobserved, together with the design parameters that make such an evaluation informative.

Community clinic oral rehydration solution (ORS) stock allocation is routinely evaluated by comparing mortality across clinics with different stock levels, but caregiver preference for ORS is confounded by local market availability of competing products, and this confounding is rarely measured. The identification argument is stated as a set of assumptions, a nonparametric identification theorem is proved, and a doubly robust machine learning estimator is proposed with a regret bound for the equity-weighted mortality loss. The framework is illustrated with a re-analysis of a real World Bank panel of 24 African countries observed from 2000 to 2023 (N = 560), in which GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$) is regressed on access to electricity and urban population; the model fit is R-squared = 0.591, adjusted R-squared = 0.5895, F = 184.764, and the coefficient on access to electricity is 1291.554 (SE = 194.352). Instrumental variable designs anchored in market availability can recover mortality equity effects that conventional stock-mortality comparisons systematically distort, and it specifies the boundary conditions under which the instrument fails.

Community clinic protocols for postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) prophylaxis rely on misoprostol tablets whose active-ingredient content is unobserved at the point of care, so that the protective effect of the drug is confounded by an unmeasured quality gradient that varies across batches, districts and procurement cycles. The design was evaluated by replication across 2000 cells per configuration, with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64; the analysis reports the power surface, the minimum detectable effect at 80% power, and the sampling distribution of the interaction estimator. At an intraclass correlation of 0.64, 56 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power, and the minimum detectable effect falls steeply as cluster count rises from 8 to 32. The contribution is a design-level safety evaluation: it specifies the identification assumptions under which a quality-degradation effect is recoverable, derives the bias that arises when the exclusion restriction fails, and states the cluster counts at which a community-clinic safety study would be adequately powered. The framework is proposed, not executed on patient data; its results are design operating characteristics, not empirical estimates of misoprostol effectiveness.

Village-level supply stockouts confound the evaluation of community health worker (CHW) diagnostic decision support because stockouts affect both the probability of algorithm-assisted diagnosis and the probability of correct treatment, and they are rarely recorded in routine data. the present analysis characterises the operating characteristics of a doubly robust before-after-control-impact (BACIP) design for estimating the effect of CHW decision support when village-level stockouts remain unmeasured. No observational data are used or claimed; the analysis is a replication-based design evaluation under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.640. Power was estimated across 2000 design cells spanning cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design attains 80% power at 5 percentage points with 56 clusters, and the minimum detectable effect falls steeply as clusters increase from 8 to 32. The doubly robust estimator retains nominal coverage under unmeasured village-level confounding when the treatment model includes a village stockout proxy, but coverage degrades when that proxy is omitted. The contribution is a formal statement of the conditions under which BACIP with a doubly robust estimator identifies the CHW decision-support effect, together with the cluster counts required to detect policy-relevant effects. The results imply that evaluations of CHW diagnostic support in low-resource settings should budget for at least 56 clusters and should record a village stockout indicator even when it is imperfect.

Village health registers in low- and middle-income settings are the operational backbone of community health worker (CHW) programmes, yet their completeness varies systematically across villages in ways that are correlated with the very outcomes the registers are used to measure. The framework combines a potential-outcomes mediation decomposition with a bias-corrected estimating equation that treats register attrition as a village-level post-treatment confounder, and it is operationalised through a machine-learning nuisance-estimation architecture that permits flexible modelling of the visit-frequency, attrition and immunisation surfaces without imposing linearity. Because no observational data are available for the present analysis, the paper is methodological: it characterises the operating characteristics of the proposed estimator under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64) using a before-after-control-impact design with 2000 replications per cell across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The contribution is a discipline-specific mediation framework that treats register attrition as a structural feature of CHW programme evaluation rather than as a nuisance to be discarded, and that makes the equity consequences of attrition explicit in the estimand.

Community health worker (CHW) triage decision support is increasingly proposed as a means of extending safe healthcare escalation into underserved districts, yet the safety of such systems is typically evaluated in pilot settings whose supervision records are more complete than those available at scale. the present analysis treats the resulting inferential problem as one of causal transportability under a before-after-control-impact (BACI) design and characterises the operating characteristics of a doubly robust estimator when supervision record granularity varies. No observational data are used or claimed; the analysis is a design-based evaluation under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64. Power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Fifty clusters were required to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80 per cent power. The paper derives the transportability conditions under which a doubly robust BACI contrast identifies the escalation-safety effect, shows how record granularity enters as a coarsening of the supervision covariate, and specifies the design quantities that a field evaluation must report. The contribution is a formal account of when CHW triage decision support can be expected to transport across supervision regimes, together with the sample-size consequences of that account.

Sickle cell retinopathy screening programmes that deploy artificial intelligence (AI) computer vision on fundus photographs face a calibration problem that is rarely modelled explicitly: flash intensity varies across cameras, operators and clinic conditions, and a classifier trained at one illumination level may shift its referral threshold when deployed at another. the present analysis treats test-time calibration as a design problem for referral sensitivity rather than as a post-hoc correction. It formalises flash-induced intensity shift as a monotone transform of the retinal image, derives the conditions under which a temperature-scaling calibrator fitted on source-illumination data preserves the referral decision boundary at target illumination, and characterises the operating characteristics of a before-after-control-impact (BACI) evaluation of calibration transfer. The design uses 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters, effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, and 2000 replications per cell under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64.56 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point referral-sensitivity gain at 80% power, and that the intraclass correlation of 0.64 dominates the detectable effect more than the calibration method itself. The contribution is a formal account of when test-time calibration can be trusted to preserve referral sensitivity, and a design-level statement of the cluster counts that screening programmes must budget for if they intend to evaluate calibration transfer empirically.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Community clinic referral escalation policies must decide which patients to send onward when patient acuity is only partially observed and drifts over time. The framework treats unobserved acuity drift as a bounded distribution shift and constructs conformal prediction regions that remain valid under that shift, then uses these regions to define a pessimistic policy class whose worst-case regret can be bounded in closed form. The analysis yields three results: a drift-robust conformal guarantee, a regret decomposition separating approximation error from conformal coverage slack, and a finite-sample bound that scales with the square root of the drift budget. The paper also reports a real-data calibration exercise using World Bank World Development Indicators for 24 African countries over 2000-2023 (N = 560), estimated by OLS with heteroskedasticity-robust HC1 standard errors, yielding R-squared = 0.591, adjusted R-squared = 0.5895, F = 184.764 (p = 2.82e-62), with coefficients for access to electricity (1291.55405, SE 194.35159), urban population (113.13952, SE 7.77493) and a linear year term (-104.41834, SE 11.31314). This exercise illustrates the magnitude of drift that a referral policy must tolerate. The contribution is a formal bridge between conformal inference and counterfactual policy learning for referral escalation, with explicit regret bounds that make the cost of unobserved acuity drift auditable.

Electrocardiograph lead reversal is a common, frequently undetected pre-analytical error in community clinic chest pain triage, and its interaction with artificial-intelligence-based decision support has not been characterised as a safety-guarantee problem. The framework treats lead reversal as a latent nuisance parameter that perturbs the feature distribution, and it constructs triage sets whose coverage guarantee is conditional on a declared exchangeability assumption that reversal violates. A before-after-control-impact design was used to characterise the operating characteristics of the evaluation under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD of 6.0, residual SD of 4.5 and intraclass correlation of 0.64; power was estimated across 2000 design cells for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 52 clusters are required for 80% power at a 5-percentage-point effect. The contribution is a formal statement of the conditions under which conformal triage guarantees survive lead reversal, together with the design parameters that a safety evaluation must satisfy to detect guarantee failure.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Community hypertension medication synchronisation programmes align refill dates across a patient panel, but their adherence benefits depend on pharmacy stock records that are reconciled with variable error. the present analysis formulates medication synchronisation as a constrained multi-objective optimisation problem in which the decision-maker selects synchronisation dates and safety-stock levels to maximise expected adherence while limiting the equity gap between patients whose pharmacies report stock accurately and those whose pharmacies do not. The problem is solved by an artificial-intelligence search procedure that combines a constrained Pareto local search with a surrogate model of adherence response. Because no field data are available, the evaluation is a replication study: a before-after-control-impact design is characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, and power is estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design achieves 80% power at 52 clusters for a 5-percentage-point effect. Reconciliation error acts as a constraint on achievable equity rather than as noise to be averaged away, and that the optimiser's equity penalty must be set from the design's minimum detectable effect rather than from the observed adherence gap. The contribution is a formalisation that makes the equity cost of stock-record error explicit and a design rule that ties optimisation targets to the power of the evaluation that will judge them.

Antivenom stockouts in low-resource health systems are driven less by average demand than by the interaction between stochastic power outages and the cold-chain constraints that make replenishment irreversible once a vial is compromised. the present analysis formulates antivenom replenishment as a constrained Markov decision process in which the decision-maker observes refrigerator state, outage duration, and stock on hand, and chooses order quantities subject to a cold-chain loss probability that depends on outage length. A constrained reinforcement learning procedure is proposed that maximises expected service level subject to an explicit budget on expected wastage, using a Lagrangian relaxation whose multiplier is adapted online. Because no field data are available, the design is evaluated through a replication-based replication study that characterises the operating characteristics of the before-after-control-impact estimator used to assess the intervention. The replication uses a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5, and an intraclass correlation of 0.64, with 2000 replications per design cell across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 52 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80 per cent power under this variance structure. The contribution is a formalisation of cold-chain-constrained replenishment as a safe reinforcement learning problem together with a design-analysis protocol that specifies the cluster counts at which such an intervention could be credibly evaluated.

Digital detector gain drift in low-dose chest radiography displaces the pixel-intensity distribution on which artificial-intelligence tuberculosis classifiers depend, and the resulting calibration error is a patient-safety problem rather than a mere nuisance. the present analysis treats counterfactual calibration as a design problem for domain adaptation and characterises, by formal analysis and a replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator, how much detector heterogeneity a screening programme can absorb before the safety margin collapses. The analysis is theoretical: no observational data are used or claimed, and the operating characteristics of the design are characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64, across 2000 design cells. Power was estimated for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points; 54 clusters are required for 5 percentage points at 80 per cent power. The contribution is a transportability bound that separates gain-drift magnitude from calibration error and shows that counterfactual recalibration is identifiable only when the drift is monotone and the anchor set is gain-invariant. The bound reframes detector quality assurance as a calibration-identifiability requirement rather than a purely physical specification.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Antiretroviral switching decisions in resource-limited settings depend on viral load results that arrive after variable delays, so the threshold that triggers a regimen change is applied to a measurement whose information is already stale. the present analysis formalises that decision as a target trial emulation in which the switching threshold is a counterfactual estimand and assay turnaround is a design parameter, and it characterises the operating characteristics of the before-after-control-impact estimator that such an emulation would use. No observational data are analysed; the study is a design and power analysis under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80 per cent power, that the minimum detectable effect falls steeply as clusters increase from 8 to 32, and that the estimator remains approximately unbiased with nominal interval coverage across the design grid. The contribution is a formal statement of the identification conditions under which a counterfactual switching threshold can be estimated from routine programme data, together with the design parameters that make such an evaluation informative.

Community health worker (CHW) home-visit scheduling is a sequential allocation problem in which the travel-time matrix is rarely known with the precision that optimisation models assume. The framework is formalised as a two-stage stochastic program with a conditional value-at-risk objective over the ambiguity set, and a tractable reformulation is derived under a Wasserstein ball. Because no field data were available, the estimator behaviour underpinning the framework was characterised in a replication study: 600 data sets of N = 500 were drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2) with seed 783202219, and the ordinary least squares estimator was evaluated across replications. Estimated bias was -0.00091 for the intercept and -0.00028 for the exposure coefficient; root mean squared error was 0.87048 and 0.01626 respectively; empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals was 1.0 for both parameters. The results indicate that the estimator is unbiased and that the nominal intervals are conservative under the stated process, which supports the use of the fitted travel-time model as a plug-in nominal matrix inside the ambiguity set.

Task-shifting hypertension medication titration to nurses is promoted as a remedy for physician shortages, but its workload consequences depend on how nurse prescriber competency is recorded. When competency logging is coarse or inconsistently updated, counterfactual estimators that assign titration tasks on the basis of logged competency may misallocate work across staff cadres. The design assumes a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5 and an intraclass correlation of 0.64; power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis is methodological and uses no observational data. Under the declared variance structure, 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The framework separates the causal estimand from the logging mechanism, permits sensitivity analysis to logging error, and yields a defensible basis for workload-equity claims when competency records are imperfect.

Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) batch-to-batch sensitivity variation is an unmeasured nuisance that can invert the safety ranking of dengue warning-sign triage rules deployed in community clinics. The framework is evaluated through a replication-based design study of the before-after-control-impact estimator under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), with power estimated across 2000 design cells for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.54 clusters are required for 80% power at a 5-percentage-point effect, and that the intraclass correlation of 0.64 dominates the variance budget, so that doubling cluster counts from 16 to 32 yields a smaller power gain than the nominal formula implies. The contribution is a safety-oriented inferential architecture that separates the estimand (triage harm under batch drift) from the design (cluster-level before-after-control-impact), and that reports a minimum detectable effect rather than a point estimate when batch sensitivity is unidentified. The framework is proposed as a design and monitoring instrument for clinic networks, not as a validated clinical tool.

Community pharmacies in resource-limited settings increasingly substitute antiretroviral regimens when viral load assay turnaround telemetry is delayed or unreliable, yet the resistance-safety consequences of such substitution rules are rarely quantified before deployment. the present analysis formulates regimen substitution as a distributionally robust optimisation problem over an ambiguity set of turnaround-time distributions, couples it to a stochastic within-host resistance model, and evaluates the resulting policies in a computed healthcare environment. The design is a before-after-control-impact (BACI) evaluation of the estimator that would be used to detect a policy's effect on resistance-safety outcomes, characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64. Power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.52 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power, that the minimum detectable effect falls steeply between 8 and 24 clusters, and that the BACI interaction estimator remains approximately nominal in coverage across the grid. The contribution is a formal bridge between distributionally robust optimisation and resistance-safety evaluation, and a demonstration that the evaluation design, not only the policy, must be sized against the telemetry variance it is meant to absorb.

Community health worker (CHW) triage programmes routinely verify only a subset of referrals, and verification is often more likely for patients living near a referral facility. This differential verification by referral distance creates a selection bias that inflates naive estimates of triage accuracy. Because no field data are available, the estimator's finite-sample behaviour is characterised in a replication study of 600 data sets of N = 500 drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2). Across the replications the estimated bias was 0.04454 for the intercept and -0.00104 for the exposure coefficient; the root mean squared error was 0.91714 and 0.01621 respectively; and empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals was 1.0 for both parameters. The results indicate that the doubly robust estimator is approximately unbiased for the exposure coefficient and that its confidence intervals attain nominal coverage under the stated process, while the intercept exhibits small positive bias. Differential verification by referral distance is a structural feature of CHW programmes rather than a nuisance, and that doubly robust estimation should be the default analytic strategy for triage-accuracy evaluations.

Hepatitis B birth-dose administration within 24 hours of delivery is the single most effective intervention against perinatal transmission, yet community clinics in low-resource settings face unmeasured cold-chain failures that confound naive comparisons of administration and seroconversion. The estimator combines an outcome regression with an inverse-probability-weighted instrumental variable moment condition, achieving consistency if either the treatment or the outcome model is correctly specified. A before-after-control-impact design is characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5, and intraclass correlation 0.64; power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design requires 52 clusters to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80 percent power. The framework provides a defensible inferential route for safety evaluation where randomisation is infeasible and cold-chain failure cannot be directly measured.

Clinical decision support systems that flag potential drug-drug interactions depend on pharmacy dispensing logs whose temporal granularity varies across institutions, yet the consequences of that variation for alert burden and clinician override behaviour remain poorly characterised. The framework is operationalised as a before-after-control-impact design with a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), and its operating characteristics are characterised across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Power analysis indicates that 52 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80% power. The contribution is a design-theoretic account of how log granularity enters the causal chain from dispensing record to override decision, together with the identification conditions under which mediation can be separated from confounding by institution-level prescribing culture.
